standard.title: Respectful relationships
standard.description: examine the roles of respect, empathy, power and coercion in developing respectful relationships
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have described and demonstrated how respect and empathy can be expressed to positively influence relationships (Y5-6). They can express respect and empathy but have not yet been expected to examine how power and coercion operate within or against respectful relationships.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students examine the roles of respect, empathy, power and coercion in developing respectful relationships.

nodes.label: Understanding the components of respectful relationships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what respect, empathy, power and coercion mean in relationship contexts and describe how each contributes to or undermines respectful relationships.
nodes.minimum_width: Define respect and empathy in a relationship context and explain how one of power or coercion can affect whether a relationship is respectful.
nodes.typical_width: Explain all four concepts (respect, empathy, power, coercion) in relationship contexts; describe how each operates differently in different relationship types (peer, family, romantic); explain how positive use of power enables rather than undermines respectful relationships.
wider: Examine what constitutes disrespectful, harmful or violent behaviour within peer, family and intimate relationships, distinguishing on a spectrum from minor disrespect to coercion and harm
Investigate how cultural norms shape expectations about respect and power in relationships, and how students navigate these norms when engaging with people from different cultural backgrounds
nodes.hinge_reason: Examination of relationship dynamics requires a conceptual framework that distinguishes between these four concepts. Students who conflate power with coercion, or who see empathy as the only positive force, cannot meaningfully examine how respectful relationships are developed and maintained.

response_modes.reason: Explicitly distinguish the four concepts using a framework before applying them to scenarios. Particularly important to clarify that power can be positive (enabling others) as well as negative (coercive) — this distinction is central to the descriptor's intent.

success_criteria: Explains what respect and empathy mean in a relationship context
Explains how power or coercion can affect whether a relationship is respectful

nodes.label: Examining relationship dynamics in context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine specific relationship scenarios and analyse how respect, empathy, power and coercion are operating, and how the dynamic changes across contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Examine one relationship scenario and identify how at least two of the four concepts (respect, empathy, power, coercion) are operating in it.
nodes.typical_width: Examine relationship dynamics across a range of contexts (alone, with friends, with family, online); analyse how behaviour changes depending on context and who is present; identify how bullying and harassment operate through these concepts.
wider: Propose strategies for addressing racism towards First Nations Australians, examining the role of bystanders in promoting respectful interactions and challenging disrespect and discrimination in everyday contexts
Analyse how online relationship dynamics create new power and coercion patterns that differ from face-to-face contexts, examining specific examples of digital disrespect and what makes them harmful

response_modes.reason: Context changes how all four concepts operate — examining across multiple relationship contexts prevents students from applying a single, context-independent model that does not account for social setting.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Examining bystander roles and cross-cultural respect connects the conceptual framework to concrete social action — students who engage here build understanding of how they can actively contribute to respectful community relationships beyond their immediate peer group.
success_criteria: Examines a relationship scenario and identifies how at least two of the four concepts are operating
Explains how context (e.g. alone vs with friends vs online) affects the dynamic

nodes.label: Developing respectful relationships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what is needed to develop and maintain respectful relationships and propose strategies for responding to disrespect, coercion or harmful behaviour.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one thing needed to develop a respectful relationship and describe one strategy for responding to a specific example of disrespect or coercive behaviour.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the conditions that develop respectful relationships (mutual respect, empathy, equitable power); propose and evaluate strategies for responding to bullying, harassment, racism and violence in peer, family and intimate contexts.
wider: Propose and evaluate bystander strategies for challenging racism and discrimination in everyday contexts, examining how bystander responses can shift norms over time
Examine how showing respect for cultural norms and sensitivities when building relationships across cultural backgrounds requires active learning, not just good intentions

response_modes.reason: Developing respectful relationships integrates all four conceptual elements into an action-oriented conclusion — instruction should help students apply the analytical framework they have built to practical relationship decisions.

success_criteria: Explains at least one condition needed to develop a respectful relationship
Proposes at least one strategy for responding to disrespect, coercion or harmful behaviour in a specific relationship context
